summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory, and the United States federal framework applies on the island in full: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. Puerto Rico's own legislation does not soften that framework, and in the area of trans medical care it sharpens it.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents may present a marker that does not match their appearance at inspection. Entry scrutiny is tightened for one category of traveller in particular: in February 2025 the United States State Department announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

Airport screening follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure at Puerto Rico's airports. All luggage is screened and may be hand-searched. Prosthetics, including breast forms, are treated as medically necessary and are not subject to the three-liquid rule, and medical equipment and prosthetics are permitted through the checkpoint after screening; published guidance for trans travellers advises packing strategies that reduce the likelihood of an invasive search.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21 and barred public funding for it. Physicians who violate the ban face up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of their medical licences. Reporting on the enactment describes a law pushed through non-public hearings and written with deliberate vagueness, so that physicians and affirming parents who facilitate hormone therapy or top surgery risk prosecution; the law also requires the education and health departments to run campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments that would have permitted puberty blockers and allowed existing hormone therapy to continue, and the enacted text did not adopt them. The report characterises the result as the most extreme care restriction in any United States jurisdiction. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

Executive Order 14168 directs federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognise only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by housing transgender inmates according to sex assigned at birth rather than asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or placed in solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people in its custody. Advocates argue that the order overrides the Prison Rape Elimination Act requirement that trans inmates' housing be determined by an individual safety assessment. These custody rules govern federal prisoners held in Puerto Rico.

Protection against bias violence exists on paper and its enforcement record is thin. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The first hate crime charges in Puerto Rico's history were brought in 2020, after Juan Pagán Bonilla confessed that he and Sean Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over the ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

General non-discrimination coverage stops short of public accommodations. House Bill 1725 passed the Puerto Rico House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation, public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass, Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House so that it applies only to employment discrimination, leaving public facilities uncovered.
tangentialFactors:
Sexual privacy and relationship recognition on the island were settled through United States federal courts rather than local legislation. Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002; after Lawrence v. Texas struck down state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts in 2003, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. Marriage equality arrived through federal litigation: four same-sex couples joined the lawsuit filed in March 2014, the Ada Conde Vidal case, with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening, and the plaintiffs included a couple married in Canada in 2007, one married in New York in 2012 and a former National Guard member.

Legislative turbulence around sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections has run in both directions for more than a decade. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 pairing of bills was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval and sustained protests.

In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.
localsOnly:
Conversion therapy for minors remains unregulated in Puerto Rico. The pro-statehood NPP caucus in the Puerto Rico House blocked a floor vote on SB1000 in March 2019, which would have banned the practice for minors despite Senate passage and governor support, with co-sponsor Senator Zoe Laboy dissenting publicly. In April 2019 Governor Alejandro García Padilla announced a pairing of SB1253, framed as clarifying religious freedom principles, with SB1254, a conversion-therapy ban carrying a pastoral exemption for clergy; LGBT council president Johanne Velez García and allies said the pairing would open doors to discrimination by licensing refusal of service on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds. The governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both bills on 13 June 2019 amid sustained opposition.

Residents also live under the July 2025 care ban and its funding bar, and under the mandate that the education and health departments run campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Ramos Otero's proposed amendments permitting puberty blockers and continuation of existing hormone therapy were not enacted, so existing patients under 21 have no statutory route to continued treatment.

Employment is the only ground of protection in force for residents: Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was narrowed in the House to employment discrimination, so public facilities, public transportation and business transactions remain outside the statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation's announced court challenge to the July 2025 care ban is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit or judicial ruling was located, so whether the territory's own corrections system has any trans-specific housing provision is unresolved rather than confirmed absent.

Beyond the 2020 prosecution arising from the murders of two transgender women, the inventory does not document how often Puerto Rico's hate crime statutes or the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act have been used in trans cases; the enforcement record after that case is not sourced.

The inventory does not state whether the state of emergency declared in January 2021 remains in force, funded or operational.
